newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Bush continue to defy caustic music critics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bush continue to defy caustic music critics.

text.p: They have not won over all the critics yet but the British rockers who make up Bush can still count on plenty of fans as they kick off a world tour promoting the band's new hit album.

Like Led Zeppelin, a band initially reviled in the music press 25 years earlier, Bush was put through the critical wringer with its 1994 debut album "Sixteen Stone." Reviews that lambasted the quartet as purveyors of a watered-down, derivative grunge sound did not stop the album from selling five million copies in the United States.

Bush's follow-up, "Razorblade Suitcase," spent two weeks at No. 1 and remains ensconced in the U.S. top 40 after 17 weeks. Its sales of 2.2 million should get a boost from a tour that will keep the band on the road until early next year.

The band also is graduating from its "cult" status back home, where such groups as Blur, Pulp and Oasis have grabbed the headlines for the past few years. "Razorblade Suitcase" peaked at No. 2 in Britain, behind the Spice Girls.
"We are England's biggest slacker export," Bush vocalist Gavin Rossdale, 29, laughs derisively about the angle in the British press. As he speaks, the BBC is filming a documentary on the band.

While bands such as Soundgarden and Pearl Jam, to whom Bush has often been unfavourably compared, have seen their latest albums fall victim to a depressed music retail sales climate, Bush seems to have thrived on it. Rossdale is proud that the band has escaped the "sophomore jinx" wherein hit groups often flop with their second album.
PEOPLE EITHER LIKE THEM OR HATE THEM

"I think it's just down to the record and down to the fact that we tour and we work it," he told Reuters. "There's no great mystery: either people like the songs and like the album, or they don't, or they don't get a chance to hear it. It takes a lot of people to make a band successful and so maybe there's more to it than meets the moment."

Rossdale, who writes all the songs, co-founded Bush in 1992 with lead guitarist Nigel Pulsford. Bass player Dave Parsons and drummer Robin Goodridge were soon added. After failing to attract much interest from British record companies they ended up at Los Angeles-based Trauma Records, which is co-owned by George Michael's former manager, Rob Kahane.

"Sixteen Stone" came out in November 1994 and caught fire with the first single, "Everything Zen." Subsequent hits such as "Machinehead" and "Glycerine" established Bush as a favourite at modern rock radio.

Along the way Rossdale emerged as a bona fide pinup and his relationship with Gwen Stefani of labelmate band No Doubt has made him a bit of a celebrity, much to his amusement. The rest of the band does not seem to mind that he inadvertently grabs the spotlight.

"I think they're pretty happy with the income and what's going on in their lives. They're smart enough to realise that that's part of it. I think that they all wanted to be on the cover of Rolling Stone with me (last April), but then when we got (beaten up) in the piece they were pretty pleased they weren't on the cover."
Nor does the rest of the band ever "give a toss" about Rossdale's rather impressionistic lyrics, he says.

"We just did a video for 'Personal Holloway' and I was going, 'Just sing some of the words,' because I think it looks really good if the band members all sing the song. And Dave couldn't. He was like, 'I don't know what the words are.'"
Rossdale says he is "probably" a millionaire by now and has spent his money on a house, a few paintings and helping out friends. The band also ploughs its money back into touring.

This time around, the band does not have to struggle to fill 90 minutes with one hour-long album. Covers such as the Sex Pistols' "Bodies" and Neil Young's "Cortez the Killer" add a new dimension to the set list.

Rossdale plans to take six months off next year when the Bush tour winds down. For now, he is eagerly awaiting a summer break in August when he will go away with Stefani -- "unless she meets some tall, dark stranger on the road and decides to live with him instead."
